rationale: Jehoshaphat's safe return follows the Lord's rescue when the Syrian charioteers surrounded him.
Jehu's rebuke addresses the marriage and military alliance through which Jehoshaphat helped Ahab.
The later alliance with Ahaziah repeats the condemned partnership and receives another prophetic announcement of its consequences.
The earlier account supplies the concrete acts commended here: seeking the Lord and removing Judah's sacred groves.
Jehoshaphat's personal tour to turn Judah back to God continues his earlier dispatch of teachers with the book of the law.
The appointment of judges city by city carries out the law requiring judges in all Israel's cities.
The judges' responsibility to the Lord restates Moses' reason for fearless judgment: judgment belongs to God.
Jehoshaphat forbids the same judicial corruption named in the law: partiality and taking gifts or bribes.
The assertion that God neither favors status nor accepts gifts echoes the law's description of God's impartial character.
Jerusalem's court of priests and ancestral leaders corresponds to the central tribunal for difficult cases at God's chosen place.
The charge to judge in God's fear with a full heart applies the law's requirement of wholehearted service to these officials.
The language about blood disputes and binding instruction closely follows the law governing difficult cases brought to the central court.
The respective priestly and ruling authorities give concrete form to the law's priest and judge whose decisions must be obeyed.
The charge to be strong and act with God present recalls David's encouragement alongside the appointed priests, Levites, and rulers.

For Moab and Ammon, named in both passages, Jehoshaphat's prayer recalls Israel's earlier restraint and describes their assault on its inheritance; no identity between Minaeans and Mount Seir is asserted.
The report of a great invading multitude directly prompts the king's fast and Judah's assembly to seek God.
The king seeks the Lord in danger in accordance with the earlier prophetic promise that returning Israel will find Him.
Judah's collective appeal at the temple enacts Solomon's provision for all Israel to pray there under enemy oppression.
Jehoshaphat stands before the temple assembly as Solomon did when inaugurating prayer from its court.
Jehoshaphat's appeal to irresistible divine power recalls Asa's prayer that no human force could prevail against the God who saves with many or few.
The appeal to the land given Abraham's descendants invokes the covenant that specifies both the land and its former peoples.
Solomon's account of building the house for God's name supplies the historical sanctuary foundation invoked in this prayer.
The petition explicitly resumes Solomon's temple prayer about famine, death, enemy oppression, and God hearing the afflicted.
The appeal for rescue before the named house also invokes Solomon's request that God hear His people when they go to war.
Moses' instructions concerning Seir and Moab explain the restraint toward those peoples that Jehoshaphat now recalls.
The prohibition on attacking Ammon supplies the third specific instance of Israel's restraint cited in the prayer.
The threatened expulsion concerns the land promised by covenant to Abraham's descendants, the basis of Jehoshaphat's complaint.
Like Asa facing an overwhelming army, Jehoshaphat acknowledges human weakness and appeals to God's power to deliver Judah.
As with Azarias addressing Asa, the Spirit comes upon a named speaker who delivers God's word to king and assembled Judah.
The declaration that the battle belongs to God closely recalls David's declaration that the Lord owns the battle and saves beyond weapons.
The promise that God will fight for His frightened people repeats the assurance Moses gave at the sea.
The promise that Judah will see the Lord's salvation without fighting recalls Moses' instruction to see God's salvation while the Lord fights.
The enemies destroy one another and Judah finds only bodies, fulfilling the promise that Judah will not have to wage this battle.
The king and people's prostration answers the Spirit-given announcement of deliverance they have just heard.
The Levites' loud praise fulfills the established Levitical duty of standing to praise and thank the Lord.
The command to trust God's prophet applies specifically to the preceding oracle promising deliverance on the next day.
The singers use the established thanksgiving refrain that God's mercy endures for ever.
Both victories are attributed to the Lord turning the enemy army's weapons against its own members.
The mutual rout carries out the oracle that the battle belongs to God and Judah will see salvation without fighting.
The coalition's attack upon itself parallels the divinely caused internal fighting in Gideon's enemy camp.
Judah's sight of the already defeated enemy supplies the promised sight of salvation without Judah waging the battle.
As after Asa's God-given victory, Judah gathers abundant livestock and other spoil from the defeated force before returning to Jerusalem.
The valley's blessing after victory completes the thanksgiving that began before the Lord routed the invaders.
The joyful return deliberately reverses the king's fear at the beginning of the invasion crisis.
The victorious procession returns to the same house where the king had appealed for God to hear and save.
The fear of God among surrounding kingdoms resumes the earlier description of divine terror protecting Jehoshaphat from war.
The rest granted after Judah seeks God repeats the outcome of the wholehearted seeking under Asa.
Kings gives the same accession age, twenty-five-year reign, and mother for Jehoshaphat, with different spellings of the names.
Both regnal assessments say Jehoshaphat followed Asa's way without turning from what was right before the Lord.
Both accounts qualify Jehoshaphat's favorable assessment by reporting the survival of the high places.
Both conclude the reign by directing readers to fuller records; Chronicles names Jehu's accounts while Kings names Judah's annals.
Kings' account of Ahaziah's Baal worship explains the lawlessness that makes Jehoshaphat's new partner objectionable.
The shipbuilding venture is the specific work that Eliezer's oracle says God has shattered through the alliance.
The prophet's condemnation of friendship with Ahaziah renews Jehu's earlier warning against helping those opposed to the Lord.
Kings also records Jehoshaphat's burial beside his fathers in David's city and Joram's succession.
The named sons of Jehoshaphat identify the brothers whom Joram subsequently murders after consolidating his rule.
The father's gifts and division of cities among his sons form the immediate background to Joram's violent elimination of his brothers.
Elijah's written accusation expressly names the murder of Joram's better brothers as a reason for the announced judgment.
Both accounts give Joram's accession age as thirty-two and his Jerusalem reign as eight years.
Both connect Joram's evil conduct in Ahab's way with his marriage to Ahab's daughter.
Joram's marriage to Ahab's daughter continues the marriage alliance earlier made between Jehoshaphat and Ahab's house.
Both explain the preservation of David's dynasty through God's promise of an enduring lamp, despite Joram's evil.
The Davidic covenant promises correction without withdrawal of mercy and an enduring house, grounding the preservation stated here.
Both place Edom's break with Judah and establishment of its own king within Joram's reign.
Kings recounts the same expedition, encirclement by Edom, strike against the enemy, and flight of the people.
Both report Edom's continuing independence and the contemporary revolt of Lomna or Lobena; Chronicles adds its theological explanation.
The prophetic accusation repeats the specific charge that Joram led Judah and Jerusalem into prostitution after Ahab's pattern.
The rebuke's contrast with Jehoshaphat and Asa rests on the earlier judgment that Jehoshaphat followed Asa in doing right.
The letter's charges correspond to the narrated murder of the brothers and Joram's adoption of Ahab's conduct.
The invaders' removal of the royal household and possessions realizes the announced blow against Joram's family and belongings.
Joram's incurable abdominal disease and fatal outcome are the narrated fulfillment of the letter's specific bodily judgment.
The Lord's stirring of foreign attackers initiates the blow against Joram's people and possessions announced in the prophetic letter.
The next accession account explains why the surviving youngest son becomes king: the invading band killed the older sons.
The incurable abdominal illness matches the particular disease foretold against Joram.
The fatal emergence of Joram's belly completes the disease judgment in the prophetic message; no duration is harmonized with another account.
Kings corroborates the accession age, reign length, death, and burial in David's city; Chronicles supplies exclusion from the royal tombs.
Both record Ahaziah's succession to Joram; Chronicles additionally explains the loss of his older brothers.
The earlier raid left only Ahaziah among Joram's sons, explaining the choice of the youngest as successor.
Both identify Athaliah as Ahaziah's mother and give a one-year reign, but the preserved accession ages differ: twenty here and twenty-two in Kings.
Both place Ahaziah in Ahab's pattern of wrongdoing; Chronicles specifies his mother's counsel as an influence.
Kings confirms the assessment of Ahaziah's evil in the way of Ahab's house; Chronicles adds the destructive role of its counselors.
Both describe Ahaziah joining Joram against Hazael at the Gilead battle and Joram being wounded.
Both recount Joram's return for treatment at Jezreel and Ahaziah's visit to the wounded king.
Kings narrates the fatal meeting with Jehu to which Ahaziah accompanied Joram, while Chronicles describes that visit as divinely brought downfall.
Jehu's anointing and commission to destroy Ahab's house explain the anointed adversary encountered in this verse.
Kings likewise records Jehu killing Ahaziah's brothers; its roadside encounter is preserved without forcing all surrounding details into one sequence.
Both report Ahaziah's death through Jehu and subsequent burial, but Chronicles' capture in Samaria differs from Kings' flight and death at Megiddo.
Both describe Athaliah's destruction of the royal offspring after the death reported to her; the differing singular and plural wording is preserved.
Both name the king's sister as the rescuer of Joash and his nurse into the bedchamber; Chronicles additionally identifies her as Jehoiada's wife.
Both place Joash hidden in the Lord's house for six years while Athaliah rules.
Both begin Jehoiada's action in the seventh year by gathering the commanders of hundreds; Chronicles supplies their personal names.
The gathering of Levites and ancestral leaders from Judah prepares the assembly that makes the covenant with the king in God's house.
Kings likewise describes Jehoiada's covenant with the assembled leaders and his presentation of the concealed king's son.
The promise that David's offspring and house will endure grounds Jehoiada's explicit appeal to the Lord's word about David's dynasty.
Both distribute Sabbath guard divisions to protect the royal restoration, though the descriptions of their stations differ.
Kings gives the corresponding division of guards among palace and temple approaches; the gate names are not treated as identical.
The restricted entry and sacred duties accord with the law distinguishing the sanctuary responsibilities of priests and Levites from those of outsiders.
Both require an armed cordon around the king, a death penalty for intrusion, and protection when he enters and leaves.
Both describe obedience to Jehoiada and the joining of Sabbath shifts for the operation; Chronicles explains that the divisions were not dismissed.
Both record Jehoiada distributing David's stored weapons from the Lord's house to equip the king's protectors.
Both describe the armed line from one side of the house to the other beside altar and temple, surrounding the king.
Both recount bringing out the king's son, placing the crown and testimony upon him, anointing him, and acclaiming his life.
Placing the testimonies upon the king accords with the law's requirement that the ruler possess and heed the law, though the ritual itself is not specified there.
Both report Athaliah hearing the running crowd and coming into the Lord's house.
Both describe the king at his station, trumpets and rejoicing, and Athaliah tearing her clothing and crying an accusation.
Both record Jehoiada's command to remove Athaliah and his insistence that she not be killed in the Lord's house.
Both place Athaliah's death at the horses' entrance to the king's house after her removal from the temple.
Both mark the restoration with a covenant that king and people should belong to the Lord.
Both describe demolishing Baal's house, destroying its cult objects, and killing its priest before its altars.
The destruction of Baal's shrine and images implements the law's demand to overthrow foreign gods' cult objects instead of serving them.
David's arrangement of Levitical service, praise, and assistance at burnt offerings supplies the earlier institution restored by Jehoiada.
The gatekeepers' exclusion of uncleanness serves the temple purification responsibilities assigned in David's organization of the ministry.
Both end the royal escort at the palace throne. Chronicles says the king was brought up into the Lord's house, while Kings says down from it; the gate descriptions also differ.
Both end Athaliah's overthrow with the people's rejoicing and the city's quiet after her execution.
Kings gives the same accession age of seven and forty-year reign, with a differently spelled name for the mother from Beersheba.
Both limit Joash's favorable conduct to the period of Jehoiada's priestly influence.
Kings describes the collection order through which Joash pursued the temple repairs proposed here.
Both recount an initial collection for repairs followed by the failure of the priestly personnel to carry out the work promptly.
Both record the king calling Jehoiada to account over the neglected temple repair project.
The contribution assigned to the Tent of Testimony provides the Mosaic precedent invoked for funding the sanctuary's work.
The earlier destruction of Baal's house shows the cult to which Athaliah's household had diverted the Lord's holy things.
Both establish a collection chest for the temple project, while preserving different descriptions of its placement and who arranged it.
The proclaimed contribution appeals to Moses' wilderness instruction assigning Israel's contribution silver to the Tent's service.
Both describe the gathering of silver into the chest until the growing amount requires the officials' attention.
Both entrust the accumulated chest money to the king's scribe and priestly oversight, with different descriptions of handling the silver.
Both transfer repair money to work supervisors who pay carpenters, builders, and stoneworkers for the Lord's house.
Kings likewise says the money supplied to the workers was used to strengthen the Lord's house.
The accounts distinguish repair spending from vessel making: Kings bars vessels from repair funds, while Chronicles describes vessels made from the remainder after completion.
Jehoiada's death marks the transition after which the rulers influence Joash to abandon the Lord and serve idols.
Jehoiada's covenant renewal and restoration of temple service specify his good toward Israel, God, and God's house.
Joash's acceptance of the rulers' counsel after Jehoiada's death explains the earlier limitation of his righteous conduct to Jehoiada's lifetime.
The Syrian victory supplies the subsequent judgment on Judah's abandonment of God and worship of idols.
The Spirit-clothed priest's warning and murder provide the specific ensuing instance of the rejected prophetic testimony described here.
The warning that forsaking the Lord brings His abandonment repeats Azarias son of Oded's earlier covenant warning without identifying the two speakers.
The servants' conspiracy is explicitly attributed to the blood of Jehoiada's son, connecting Joash's murder order with his own violent death.
Joash's rescue and concealment by Jehoiada's wife illustrate the family's mercy that the king fails to remember when killing its son.
The dying appeal for divine judgment is followed by Joash's death in a conspiracy expressly motivated by the murdered priest's blood.
Both accounts describe a Syrian threat to Jerusalem under Joash and wealth going to the Syrian king, but their attack and tribute details remain distinct.
Asa's small-or-great army prayer ends in God's victory for Judah, while here abandoned allegiance reverses the outcome and Judah's large army loses to a few.
Both record servants conspiring to kill Joash and burial in David's city; Chronicles adds his illness, the motive, and exclusion from the royal tombs.
Kings also names the servants responsible for Joash's death, but its personal and parental names differ and are not silently equated letter for letter.
Both conclude Joash's reign by referring to written royal records and naming Amaziah as successor; Chronicles' five assailants detail is not harmonized.
Both give Amaziah's accession at twenty-five, twenty-nine-year reign, and mother from Jerusalem, with a spelling difference in her name.
Both qualify Amaziah's favorable assessment: Chronicles notes his incomplete heart, while Kings contrasts him with David and records remaining high places.
Both recount Amaziah executing his father's killers after firmly establishing his kingdom.
The preceding account identifies the servants' murder of Joash that Amaziah now punishes.
Both record sparing the killers' sons and expressly appeal to the Mosaic rule of individual liability.
The quoted prohibition of putting parents to death for children or children for parents reproduces this law of personal responsibility.
Amaziah's count by ancestral houses of men aged twenty upward able to go to war follows the basic pattern of the Mosaic military census.
The hired force and its hundred talents become the specific expenditure Amaziah questions before obeying the command to dismiss the force.
The warning against relying on Israel's army parallels the earlier rebuke of Asa's reliance on a foreign king instead of the Lord.
The later defeat demonstrates the prophet's warning that the Lord can rout Amaziah, even though that later battle has its own stated cause in idolatry.
The king's question concerns the precise hundred talents already paid for the Israelite troops, clarifying the cost of obeying the prophet.
The dismissal and anger of the Ephraimite soldiers explain why the rejected contingent subsequently attacks Judah's cities.
Kings likewise credits Amaziah with killing ten thousand Edomites; the place designations are preserved without forcing their spellings to agree.
Kings' capture of the Rock belongs to the parallel Edomite campaign, while the execution of ten thousand captives is a distinct detail supplied by Chronicles.
The raiders are the troops previously dismissed in anger, directly connecting the damaging raid with the rejected alliance.
Amaziah keeps and worships the defeated people's gods, the opposite of the destruction and rejection of cult images prescribed in the Canaan conquest law.
Amaziah's worship of Seir's gods contrasts with the command, given for entering Canaan, to overthrow the nations' cult objects instead of bowing to or serving their gods.
The prophet exposes the contradiction between Amaziah's defeat of Seir and his subsequent worship of gods unable to save that people.
Amaziah's rejection of the prophet's counsel is followed by the stated divine purpose to hand him over and his defeat by Israel.
Both record Amaziah sending the same challenge to Joash of Israel to meet face to face.
Both preserve Joash's Lebanon plant fable about a marriage demand and a lowly plant trampled by wild animals; the plant terms differ.
Both interpret Amaziah's Edomite victory as a source of pride and warn him to stay home lest he bring Judah down with him.
Kings likewise says Amaziah refused to listen; Chronicles adds the purpose of judgment for seeking Edomite gods.
Both place the encounter between Joash and Amaziah at Baithsamys in Judah.
Both report Judah's defeat before Israel and each man's flight to his dwelling.
Both describe Amaziah's capture and the demolition of four hundred cubits of wall between the Ephraim and Corner gates.
Both recount removal of temple and palace wealth and people called sons of mixed unions or company, followed by the return to Samaria; the terms are preserved.
Both state that Amaziah outlived Joash of Israel by fifteen years.
Both close Amaziah's record by referring readers to fuller royal records, with different descriptions of the book.
Both recount a conspiracy in Jerusalem, Amaziah's flight to Lachish, and his killing there by pursuers.
Both say Amaziah's body was transported on horses and buried with his fathers in David's city.
Both report the people's installation of Amaziah's sixteen-year-old son; Chronicles calls him Uzziah and Kings Azariah in these passages.
Both connect the new king with building Ailath or Ailoth and restoring it to Judah after the previous king's death.
Both give the ruler's age of sixteen, fifty-two-year reign, and mother Chalia from Jerusalem.
Both assess the king as doing right in accordance with his father Amaziah's conduct.
As Joash's good conduct is tied to Jehoiada's lifetime, Uzziah's seeking God is associated with the guidance of Zacharias, a distinct counselor.
The next statement identifies God's strengthening as the explanation for Uzziah's successful campaigns against the foreigners described here.
The divine help behind Uzziah's victories is recalled at the turning point where his resulting strength becomes destructive pride.
The spread of Uzziah's fame and increasing strength reappear immediately before the account turns to the pride that his strength produces.
Uzziah's building at Jerusalem's Corner Gate follows the damage to the wall reaching that gate during his father Amaziah's defeat.
The statement that Uzziah was helped until strong supplies the immediate contrast with his lifted heart once strong.
Uzziah's pride and violation of sanctuary duties exemplify the royal dangers the law addresses by requiring obedience and a heart not lifted above others.
The incense altar's daily service is assigned to Aaron, explaining why the king's attempt to burn incense intrudes upon priestly service.
The priests who follow Uzziah into the sanctuary act within the Aaronic responsibility to guard the holy things and altar against incursions that bring guilt and wrath.
The priests' insistence that the altar service belongs to Aaron's sons invokes the law assigning priesthood to them and barring outsiders.
Aaron's duty to burn morning and evening incense directly supports the priests' objection to Uzziah's attempt to perform that rite.
Kings also attributes the king's lifelong leprosy to the Lord's touch; Chronicles supplies the censer, confrontation, and forehead lesion setting.
The priests' recognition of head leprosy and removal of Uzziah correspond to priestly diagnosis of such lesions and required separation of the unclean.
Both report the king's lifelong leprosy, residence in the house of Apphousoth, and Jotham's governance of the people.
Uzziah's separate residence and exclusion while leprous accord with the law that the afflicted person remain unclean and dwell apart.

Both refer readers to fuller records of this reign. Chronicles attributes Uzziah's acts to Jessias the prophet, while Kings directs readers to Judah's royal chronicles; the two works are not identified with one another.
Both report the king's death, burial with his fathers, and Jotham's succession; Chronicles qualifies the burial as in the royal burial field because of leprosy.
